notes.text:
A FLAG IS A STATE YOU DIDN'T DRAW.

Three states on the canvas. Run 'open enter' and it rejects; run 'takeKey open enter' and it accepts. Same two states, same arrow, different answer — so the machine is remembering something the picture does not show.

Step either run and watch the Flags row: hasKey flips, and the same drawn state 'hall' appears twice with two different valuations. That is the hidden state, live.

To see it as states, open Algorithms → Hierarchical → HSM → NFA (Flatten): hall and room have each split in two, one copy per valuation of hasKey. The guard has been compiled into the state space, which is the only place a finite automaton can keep anything.

The left panel says the price out loud, as the number it actually is: drawn states → flat states.

WHY THE VARIABLES ARE BOOLEAN, AND ONLY BOOLEAN.

n flags is 2^n valuations — finite, so state x valuation is finite, so the language is still regular. Exponentially more succinct than drawing the copies, and not one word more powerful.

Change it to 'health < 20' and that argument collapses. An integer variable is an infinite state space; two of them is a two-counter machine, which is Turing-complete. That is not a statechart with a nicer guard, it is a different model wearing the same picture.

When you genuinely need to count, you have left the class — and Counter and NPDA are waiting in the model picker.

meta.title: Guards: a flag is a state you didn't draw
meta.blurb: Boolean flags let one arrow stand for a condition instead of a state. Flattening compiles them back into states — one copy per valuation — which is both why guards are succinct and why they add no power. Keeping the variables finite is what keeps the language regular.
